coredata.dc:description: In recent years, nanozymes have become promising alternatives to natural enzymes owing to their high catalytic efficiency, substrate specificity, and mild reaction conditions. The catalytic performance of nanozymes can be further improved by doping heterogeneous metals to provide high redox potentials. However, nanozymes for the degradation of endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) have been scarcely studied, and the degradation mechanisms remain unclear. Herein, a series of aminoclays (ACs) containing various metal dopants were prepared and employed for the degradation of phenolic compounds. The as-synthesized ACs with a Cu-Mn molar ratio of 1:7 (CuMnAC-1–7) showed excellent stability and superior activity for oxidizing bisphenol A (BPA) than natural laccases owing to the electron transport between Cu2+/Cu+ and Mn4+/Mn3+ in the nanozyme. The catalytic oxidation process of BPA consists of a non-free radical pathway mediated by Mn3+, as well as a free radical pathway facilitated by superoxide radicals (O2 ·-) and singlet oxygen (1O2). Specifically, Mn3+ deprived the electrons of the BPA benzene ring to form phenolic hydroxyl radicals, which were then polymerized to BPA dimers. Cu+ in the structure reduced Mn4+ to Mn3+, accelerating the electron deprivation of BPA and promoting the polymerization reaction. Finally, the high-charge-density region on the dimeric benzene ring tended to lose electrons and form free radicals, facilitating the polymerization into trimers and tetramers. The CuMnAC-1–7 could remove 95% of BPA at a concentration of 200 mg/L within 1 h under acidic conditions. This study provides a new strategy to design high-performance laccase nanozymes for EDCs degradation.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: In recent years, nanozymes have become promising alternatives to natural enzymes owing to their high catalytic efficiency, substrate specificity, and mild reaction conditions. ce:section.ce:para: Despite the convenience and benefits of plastic materials, their white pollution has threatened the ecological environment and human health in recent decades [11]. As a synthetic polymer that has been mass-produced since the early 1950 s, plastics are subjected to slow aging and degradation, eventually generating small plastic particles of less than 5 mm. These microplastics (MPs) are easily accessible to a wide range of organisms and can transfer into the human body via the food chain [60] [12]. The monomers and oligomers released by MPs during aging may become potential sources of persistent organic pollutants [37]. The stability and persistence of MPs in the environment make them difficult to degrade biologically or chemically. Moreover, MPs have complex sources, and their composition and structure depend on the sources and environmental conditions, which further increases the difficulty to investigate their degradation products [39,55].

Polycarbonate (PC) is a highly valuable engineering plastic used in electrical and electronic products owing to its outstanding impact resistance, electrical insulation, and optical performance [1]. It is one of the most abundant polymers, accounting for 26% of all polymer consumption. Some studies have reported that PC products may release bisphenol A (BPA) into seawater and freshwater resources [2]. BPA belongs to the endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) family and is widely used in the production of plastics and epoxy resins. BPA, MPs, polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), and other persistent organic pollutants in the marine environment can form organic pollution spheres, causing continuous damage to the environment [34]. In addition, BPA can leak from plastic products into food and water, resulting in a profound effect on organisms as an endocrine disruptor and further threatening the reproductive system in the human body through breathing, digestion, or skin contact, even at low concentrations [71]. Therefore, it is crucial to find an economical and effective means to reduce and eliminate BPA in the environment.

Current methods to remove BPA include adsorption, photocatalytic degradation, phytoremediation, electrocatalytic oxidation, and biodegradation. Compared to traditional physical or chemical processes, which are expensive and have hazardous byproducts, biological strategies are considered more viable [17,25,30,40,57,62]. In particular, enzyme-based treatments have gained increasing attention owing to their mild reaction conditions, nontoxic byproducts, high catalytic activity, and environmental friendliness [35,36,63]. As a member of the multicopper oxidase (MCO) family, laccase is an environmental-friendly and versatile biocatalyst for bioremediation because it can catalyze the single-electron oxidation with oxygen as the final electron acceptor and water as the only byproduct [19]. In addition, laccases catalyze the oxidative polymerization of aromatic compounds using hydrogen peroxide or oxygen as oxidants [38]. However, natural laccases are susceptible to structural changes in acidic, alkaline, or high-temperature environments and lose their catalytic activities. With the development of nanomaterial technology and supramolecular chemistry, nanozyme has emerged as a promising alternative to mimic the properties of natural enzymes. Unlike natural enzymes that only retain their activity in a specific temperature and pH range [50,52], nanozymes remain active in a wide range of environmental conditions and demonstrate durability and storage stability. Furthermore, nanozymes can be easily extracted from the reaction media for subsequent utilization. Therefore, nanozymes have found broad applications in biosensing (Li et al., 2023; [23,26,44]), environmental treatment [27,51], and biomedical devices [3,10,21].

By imitating the active center of laccase, laccase-like nanozymes have been studied as efficient alternatives to natural laccases to degrade phenolic compounds in EDCs. However, previously reported laccase-like nanozymes are exclusively copper-based materials with copper atoms as the active sites [14,28,47,49,58]. During the catalytic process, the interactive redox reaction between monovalent and divalent copper (Cu2+/Cu+) is crucial for shuttling electrons from the reduced substrates to oxygen [15,16]. In view of the synergistic effect between natural enzymes and coenzyme factors, doping other metals into copper-based nanozymes is regarded as an effective way to improve catalytic performance. The synergistic effect of the polyvalent metals and the conduction of electrons between the internal metal ions can increase the number of active sites and provide additional recognition sites. Luo et al., [24,46,56]. Given that the research on the degradation of EDCs by laccase-like nanozymes is limited, it is essential to rationally design and synthesize novel bimetallic laccase-like nanozymes.

Talc-like layered organosilicates grafted with aminoclays (ACs) with aminopropyl groups have attracted considerable attention because of their strong dispersion, substrate affinity, and excellent structural regularity and catalytic activities [8,48]. In addition, their catalytic properties can be modulated by changing the species of the central ions. In this work, a series of multivalent ACs were synthesized, and their laccase-like properties were systematically investigated. The as-synthesized ACs with a Cu-Mn molar ratio of 1:7 (CuMnAC-1–7) showed excellent laccase-like activity and was selected for the BPA degradation and mechanism investigation ( Scheme 1). This study paves the way for the design and construction of bimetallic laccase-like nanozymes for the catalytic oxidation of phenolic pollutants and provides insights into laccase-catalyzed oxidation and polymerization of aromatic compounds.

Laccase (≥1 U/mg) was purchased from Bomei Biotech Co., LTD. Copper chloride dihydrate (CuCl2·2 H2O, 99%), ferric chloride hexahydrate (FeCl3·6 H2O, 98%), zinc dichloride (ZnCl2, 98%), manganese dichloride tetrahydrate (MnCl2·4 H2O, 99%), cerium nitrate hexahydrate (Ce(NO3)3·6 H2O, 99.5%), sodium dihydrogen phosphate dihydrate (NaH2PO4·2 H2O, 99%), disodium hydrogen phosphate dodecahydrate (Na2HPO4·12 H2O, 99%), absolute ethanol (CH3CH2OH, 99.8%), tertiary butanol (TBA, (CH3)2CHOH, 99%) and ammonium oxalate monohydrate (AO, (NH4)2C2O4·H2O, 99.5%) were produced by Chengdu Kelong Chemical Reagent Co., LTD. 3-Aminopropyl triethoxysilane (APTES, C9H23NO3Si, 99%), 2,4-dichlorophenol (2,4-DP, C6H4Cl2O, 98%), 4-Aminoantipyrine (4-AP, C11H13N3O, 98%), BPA (C15H16O2, 99%), 1,4-Benzoquinone (BQ, C6H4O2, 99%) and 2,2,6,6-Tetramethylpiperidine (TEMP, 97%) were purchased from Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., LTD. All chemical reagents are of analytical grade unless stated otherwise. The ultrapure Milli-Q water (resistance>18.2 MΩ·cm) was used to prepare all buffers and solutions.

According to the literature, ten different types of ACs were synthesized by a similar strategy magnesium aminoclays (MgAC). Mendes et al., [29,41] Different proportions of copper salts and other metal salts (Table S1) were dissolved under ultrasound in a 500 mL conical flask containing 200 mL of ethanol solution. 13 mL of 3-aminopropyl triethoxysilane (APTES, Macklin Biochemical Co., LTD.) was subsequently dropped into the above solution and mixed for 5 min, then a dark paste was obtained immediately. After a further 16 h reaction in production, the precipitated ACs were centrifuged at 8000 rpm for 10 min, washed three times with ethanol (50 mL) to remove excess reactants, and dried in an oven at 50 °C for 24 h. The harvested ACs were powdered with a pestle and mortar before experiments.

The morphologies and microstructures of the as-prepared samples are observed by scanning electron microscope (SEM; Ultra 55, Zeiss, Berlin, Germany). Transmission electron microscope (TEM) imaging and elemental mapping were performed on a Libra 200 TEM equipped with high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) detector at an acceleration voltage of 200 kV. (Zeiss, Berlin, Germany). The absorption spectra of the samples are collected using a UV–visible spectrophotometer (UV-2800A, Unico, Franksville, WI, USA). The crystal structures are performed by X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns using an X 'pert Pro diffractometer (PANalytical, Eindhoven, Netherlands) with Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 1.5178 A, 40 kV × 40 mA) in the 2θ range from 2–70º. Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectra are recorded using a Spectrum One spectrometer (PerkinElmer, Waltham, MA, USA). The content of Cu and Mn were measured using inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometer (ICP-OES, Optima 8300, USA), The organic functional groups in the ACs are determined by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) using an XPS spectrometer (Escalab 250Xi, Thermo Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) with a monochromatic Al Kα source. The electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) analysis was conducted on a Bruker EMX spectrometer to determine the oxidation species with 5,5-dimethyl-1-pyrroline N-oxide (DMPO) and 2,2,6,6-tetramethyl-4-piperidinol (TEMPO) as the spin-trapping agents. The electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) analysis was performed using a Bruker Magnetic Resonance A300 spectrometer to ascertain the oxidation species, employing 2,2,6,6-tetramethyl-4-piperidinol (TEMPO) and 5,5-dimethyl-1-pyrroline-N-oxide (DMPO) as spin-trapping agents. The final products were determined by liquid chromatograph mass spectrometer (LC-MS) using a single-stage quadrupole mass spectrometer (Varian 1200LC/MS) equipped with an electrospray ion source and an atmospheric pressure chemical ion source.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Evaluation of laccase-mimicking activity of ACs
ce:section.ce:para:
The laccase-like activity of the synthesized ACs was determined by the oxidation of 2,4-dichlorophenol (2,4-DP). Concretely, 500 μL of 2,4-DP (1.0 mg/mL), 500 μL of 4-AP (1.0 mg/mL) and 500 μL of ACs (1.0 mg/mL, aqueous suspension) were added into 3.5 mL of Tris-HCl buffer (0.05 M, pH = 7.5), the solution was mixed evenly and reacted at 25 ℃ for 20 min. Then the reaction liquid was centrifuged in 10000 r/min for 1 min, and the absorbance of the supernatant was measured at 510 nm to survey the laccase-like activity (ʋ), the formula is as follows:
ʋ = [A510/(εL)]·V/t·V′

Where ε is the extinction coefficient (13.6 mM−1 cm−1) of the product, L is the optical path length (1 cm), t is the reaction time (20 min), V is the volume of the reaction liquid (5 mL), V ' is the volume of the catalyst solution.

The 2.4-DP solutions with a series of concentration gradients (0.1–1.0 mg/L) were prepared, 500 μL of each solution was added into 3.5 mL of Tris-HCl buffer (0.05 M, pH = 7.5), 500 μL of 4-AP (1.0 mg/mL) and 500 μL of ACs (1.0 mg/mL, aqueous suspension) in turn. The absorbance of the reaction product at wavelength of 510 nm was recorded after the 20 min of reaction, to calculate the reaction rate (V0), the V0 values were then plotted as a function of substrate concentration ([S]) and fitted to the Michaelis-Menten equation to obtain the kinetic parameters (Vmax and Km). Lineweaver-Burk curves were plotted as the reciprocal of the substrate concentration and the reciprocal of the initial speed of the enzyme reaction.
V0 = (Vmax × [S]) / (Km + [S])
Where V0 is the apparent initial catalytic rate, Km is the apparent Michaelis-Menten constant, Vmax is the maximum apparent initial reaction rate, and [S] is the substrate concentration.

To investigate the effect of pH, laccase or laccase nanozyme (CuMnAC-1–7) were incubated in buffer with series of pH values (pH 3–9) for 8.0 h to assess the catalytic activity (Section 2.4) and compared with the relative activities of initial laccase nanozyme and laccase. To evaluate the thermal stability, the activity of the laccase nanozyme or laccase in water was evaluated after 1.0 h of treatment at different temperatures range from − 20 to 100 °C. Similarly, the laccase nanozyme or laccase was dispersed in water (1.0 mg/mL) and stored at room temperature for 12 days, during this period, the remaining activity was measured at predetermined time intervals. The recyclability of the laccase nanozyme was tested by the centrifugation handle for recovery and carry out the determination of residual activity.

Degradation of BPA was performed in a glass vial containing laccase or laccase nanozyme and BPA. In typical cases, 0.2 mL of BPA (5.0 mg/mL, ethanol) was added into 4.8 mL of PB buffer (0.2 M, pH 7.0) containing 5.0 mg of laccase nanozyme or laccase. The resulting mixture was reacted for 24 h at room temperature with gentle stirring of 400 r/min. Then, 1.0 mL of the reaction mixture was sampled and centrifuged to remove the catalyst, the supernatant was extracted with a needle to recover the residual BPA and analyzed by High Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC) to obtain the degradation rate. HPLC analysis was performed on an Eclipse Plus C18 column (5 µm, 4.6 × 250 mm), Agilent 1260 series chromatographic system with methanol/water (60: 40, isovolumetric elution, 1.0 mL/min) as the mobile phase, the signal was monitored with a UV detector at 277 nm.

The ACs were synthesized by a one-step sol-gel method, and their crystal structures were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD). As shown in Fig. S1a, the diffraction peak around 2θ = 5º represents the (001) crystal plane with a lattice spacing between 1.65 nm and 1.99 nm. Besides, CuAC has diffraction peaks at 2θ = 10.1º, 24.1º and 32.2º, corresponding to d002 = 0.87 nm, d020, 110 = 0.37 nm and d130, 200 = 0.25 nm, respectively. MnAC shows the diffraction peaks at 2θ = 15.4º, 24.37º and 31.85º attributed to d002 = 0.57 nm, d020, 110 = 0.36 nm and d130, 200 = 0.28 nm, respectively. The XRD patterns of CuAC and MnAC indicate their 1:1 lamellar silicate structure.

The functional groups within the AC structures were analyzed by Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR). As shown in Fig. S1b, the spectra of all ACs show peaks of -N-H- (3399 cm−1), -CHX (3042 cm−1, 2929 cm−1), -NH3 + (2035 cm−1), -NH2 (1615 cm−1), -CH2 (1492 cm−1), Si-C (1123 cm−1), Si-OH (1046 cm−1), -C-N- (688 cm−1), metal-O-Si (∼650 cm−1), and metal-O (∼570 cm−1). The spectra suggest that the characteristic functional groups of layered organic silicates are retained in the ACs, and the metal ions are successfully bonded in the organosilicate structure. In addition, the strength of the metal-O bond depends on the bimetal ratio.

CuMnAC-1–7 is a layered organosilicate nanozyme synthesized by a one-step sol-gel method using Cu (II) and Mn (II) precursors at room temperature (Fig. S2). SEM ( Fig. 1a) and TEM (Fig. 1b) images show that CuMnAC-1–7 has a layered structure. The distribution of each element on the surface was investigated through HAADF. The relevant elemental mapping images show that Cu, Mn, O, Si, and N are uniformly distributed on the surface (Fig. 1c-h). The Mn content is significantly higher than that of Cu, consistent with the molar ratio of Cu and Mn in the precursors. The concentrations of Mn and Cu in CuMnAC-1–7 were 12.04 mM/g and 1.74 mM/g determined by ICP-OES, and the molar ratio of Mn and Cu was 6.91:1, consistent with the theoretical value (Table S2).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Screening the laccase-like activity of ACs
ce:section.ce:para: The above characterizations show that the as-synthesized ACs are layered silicates containing transition metals as active centers. Subsequently, the laccase-like catalytic activities of the ACs were systematically investigated using 2,4-DP as the model substrate. According to the method described in Section 2.4, the laccase-like activity of ACs was screened in Section 3.3, and the catalytic kinetic parameters of CuMnAC-1–7 were measured in Section 3.4. In the presence of laccase or laccase nanozymes, the 2,4-DP can be oxidized to a quinone intermediate, which further reacts with 4-AP to yield a Burgundy product ( Fig. 2a).

The laccase-like activity was evaluated using CuMnAC-1–7 as a model nanozyme. As shown in Fig. 2b, the mixture of 2,4-DP and 4-AP exhibits no significant color change in the absence of the catalyst. After adding CuMnAC-1–7, the mixture gradually turns wine red, and the absorbance at 510 nm gradually increases, indicating that 2,4-DP is catalyzed by CuMnAC-1–7 under the complexation of 4-AP. After reacting for 20 min, CuMnAC-1–7 generates a significantly more intense absorption peak at 510 nm than the natural laccase at an identical mass concentration (0.1 mg/mL), demonstrating its excellent laccase-like activity.

As shown in Fig. 2c, the oxidation ability of 2,4-DP in the synthesized ACs is greater than that in the natural laccase. Moreover, CuMnAC-1–1 shows the strongest laccase-like catalytic activity compared to the other nanozymes at the same concentration, indicating that doping Mn can improve the laccase-like catalytic activity of the original CuAC. In contrast, doping Zn, Fe, or Ce shows limited promoting effects. The possible reason for the effective Mn doping may be related to the electron transfer behavior between Cu and Mn ions. The Mn element has various valence states and a high redox potential. The redox potential of the Mn2+/Mn3+ electric pair is 1.51 V compared to the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE), while the potential of the T1 copper center in natural laccase is 0.8 V vs. SHE. The synergistic interaction between Cu and Mn ions promotes the catalytic oxidation of 2,4-DP and enhances the laccase-like activity.

Subsequently, the effect of the Cu:Mn molar ratio on the laccase-like activity of CuMnAC nanozymes was investigated. As shown in Fig. 2d, the CuMnAC-1–7 exhibits higher laccase-like catalytic activity for the oxidation of 2,4-DP than the other nanozymes, thus the molar ratio of Cu to Mn is set to 1:7 in the following experiments. In addition, the laccase-like activity of MnAC is significantly lower than that of CuMnAC, indicating that the catalytic activity of CuMnAC is due to the synergistic interaction between Cu and Mn.

Fig. 3a-d show that the absorbance of 2,4-DP oxidation products increases and reaches a plateau as the concentration of 2,4-DP increases for both CuMnAC-1–7 and natural laccases. When the substrate concentration is linearly related to the reaction rate, the Michaelis-Menten equation can be used to calculate the Michaelis constant (K m) and the maximum initial rate (V max) of the reaction [61]. The K m refers to the substrate concentration required to achieve half of the maximum initial reaction rate and reflects the affinity between the catalyst and substrate, and a smaller K m value indicates a stronger affinity. The Vmax is related to the activity of the enzyme. Under the same reaction conditions, the V max value of CuMnAC-1–7 is 32.19 μM/min, higher than that of natural laccase (1.18 μM/min), indicating that CuMnAC-1–7 has a higher catalytic efficiency. In contrast, the K m value of CuMnAC-1–7 is calculated as 0.63 mM, higher than that of laccase (0.13 mM). The low affinity of CuMnAC-1–7 is attributed to its specificity towards particular atomic and surface ligands, and the intricate nature of the reaction pathway has a negative impact on its affinity towards the substrate [64].

In addition to catalytic activity, stability and recyclability are important indicators to evaluate the applicability of nanozymes. The stability and recyclability of CuMnAC-1–7 under different pHs, temperatures, and storage times were investigated according to the method described in Section 2.6. Different from the catalytic activity of natural laccases, which decreases both in low- and high-temperature conditions, CuMnAC-1–7 shows high catalytic stability at various temperatures ( Fig. 4a). This is mainly due to its relatively stable metal-O structure. In addition, the electron transfer between Cu and Mn ions is promoted at high temperatures, thus maintaining the balance of electrical pairs within the crystal structure, which is conducive to catalytic reactions [22]. At different pHs, the catalytic activity of CuMnAC-1–7 significantly increases under acidic conditions and decreases in alkaline solutions. On the contrary, as the pH changes from acidic to alkaline, the catalytic activity of natural laccase increases constantly. In an acidic solution, Mn exists at its high valence state with a high redox potential, and the Cu element can maintain its stable structure, which are conducive to the improvement of the catalytic activity. In an alkaline environment, the doped Mn ions tend to precipitate as Mn(OH)2, decreasing the structural stability of CuMnAC-1–7 (Fig. 4b).

To further explore the advantages of the as-prepared CuMnAC-1–7 over natural laccases, its storage stability was evaluated. The results show that the catalytic activities of both natural laccase and CuMnAC-1–7 gradually decrease with the extension of storage time. After storage for 12 days, the relative activity of natural laccase is less than 20%, while CuMnAC-1–7 remains at approximately 70%, indicating that CuMnAC-1–7 has better storage stability (Fig. 4c). Due to the strong water solubility of natural laccase, it cannot be recycled. In contrast, the catalytic performance of CuMnAC-1–7 retains at 87% after eight cycles (Fig. 4d), indicating its superior reusability as a synthetic laccase nanozyme. Considering the high production cost of laccase catalysts, the recyclability of CuMnAC-1–7 offers additional advantages over natural laccases.

Normally, natural laccases exhibit high BPA degradation performance under appropriate conditions; however, their applications are limited by non-reusability, poor environmental adaptability, and low stability. Therefore, nanozymes are promising cadidates to degrade BPA more effectively and economically. Based on the above experimental results, CuMnAC-1–7 was selected as the nanozyme for BPA degradation. As shown in Fig. S3, the peak area of BPA is significantly reduced after the degradation is catalyzed by CuMnAC-1–7. Several new peaks related to degradation products emerge, indicating that CuMnAC-1–7 possesses good catalytic activity for BPA removal. Subsequently, the degradation efficiency of CuMnAC-1–7 was compared with that of natural laccase at the same concentration. As indicated in Fig. 5a, the degradation rate of CuMnAC-1–7 is 91.3% after 24 h, higher than that of natural laccase (80.7%), in accordance with the laccase-like activity evaluation in Section 3.2. Moreover, the initial reaction rate (V0) at different substrate concentrations was calculated, and the curve was successfully fitted to the Michaelis-Menten kinetic model (Fig. 5b), implying that the degradation of BPA by CuMnAC-1–7 conforms to the laccase-like behavior.

In this study, we investigated the factors affecting BPA degradation, including temperature, pH, nanozyme concentration, and substrate concentration. The effect of pH on the catalytic performance of CuMnAC-1–7 was shown in Fig. 6a. The BPA degradation rate of CuMnAC-1–7 reaches 95.1% after 1 h at pH 3; the rate reduces to over 90% after 24 h at pH 7 and to 4.2% after 24 h at pH 11. The Mn ion in CuMnAC-1–7 exists at its high valence state with a high redox potential under acidic conditions, which is conducive to the exposure of the active sites of the catalyst [33]. In addition, different acidic and alkaline environments can change the chemical form of BPA and thereby affect the oxidation of catalysts. When the pH was lower than the dissociation constant of BPA (pKa = 9.62), most BPA in the solution exists in its neutral form and can be adsorbed via hydrogen bonding. As the solution pH further increases, the neutral BPA gradually loses its proton to form BPA− at pH values near pKa1 (9.62), and further to BPA2− at pH values near pKa2. Due to the weak basicity of the phenoxy in the structure of BPA, its oxidation activity may be reduced after deprotonation, as the deprotonated phenoxy is less reactive towards oxidation. Cai et al., [4,7] Then, the influence of reaction temperature on the degradation rate was evaluated. When the temperature is raised from 20 °C to 70 °C, the degradation rate of BPA gradually increases from 74.0% to 99.3%, indicating that the number of activated molecules increases at high temperatures to promote the degradation of BPA. Moreover, because the stable metal-O bond in the nanozyme structure is less affected by temperature, an increase in the environmental temperature can promote electron transfer between the Cu and Mn electric pair, which also improves the catalytic activity of CuMnAC-1–7 [54] (Fig. 6b).

The influence of the nanozyme concentration reveals that the degradation rate of BPA increases from 32.7% to 80.0% when the nanozyme concentration changes from 0.1 to 2.0 mg/mL (Fig. 6c). When the concentration of nanozymes reaches 1.5 mg/mL, the BPA degradation rate tends to be stable because the excess nanozyme depletes the active sites in contact with the reaction substrate and cannot further promote the catalytic efficiency. In environmental water bodies, the concentration of BPA may be approximately 0.4 mg/L. At this concentration, the effect of catalysts on pollutants may be difficult to manifest. Therefore, we need to increase the concentration of pollutants under laboratory conditions to observe the catalytic effect. Fig. 6d indicates that the BPA degradation rate increases from 68.4% to 79.8% when the initial concentration of BPA changes from 50 to 300 mg/L. The interaction between CuMnAC-1–7 and the substrate is strengthened at a high BPA concentration, which is conducive to offsetting the effects of steric hindrance and diffusion resistance [19]. However, the BPA degradation rate decreases remarkably upon further increasing the initial concentrations of BPA to 500 and 1000 mg/L because insufficient catalysts are available in the reaction system to oxidize the substrate [63].

ce:section.ce:section-title: Reaction mechanism and elementary reaction steps
ce:section.ce:para: With the growing concerns of EDCs on human health and aquatic ecosystems, research on laccase bioremediation has greatly increased, and many studies have reported that immobilized laccases or laccase nanozymes show excellent oxidative degradation and mineralization properties for BPA [18,19,53]. Generally, the degradation of BPA involves two main routes. One is oxidative decomposition, in which BPA eventually decomposes into smaller molecules, such as CO2 and H2O [13]. The other is catalytic polymerization, wherein BPA aggregates into organic matter with a high molecular weight [45]. However, few studies have focused on the degradation of BPA using laccase-like nanozymes. Hence, the as-synthesized CuMnAC-1–7 was selected as the laccase-like nanozyme to study the degradation reaction route of BPA.

To elucidate the roles of Cu and Mn in the degradation of BPA, XPS was employed to explore the metal valence states of CuMnAC-1–7 before and after the reaction. As shown in Fig. 7a, the survey spectra display signals of Cu 2p, Mn 2p, O 1 s, and C 1 s, consistent with the elemental mapping images. The high-resolution XPS spectra of Cu 2p in Fig. 7b reveal the coexistence of Cu (I) and Cu (II) on the surface, suggesting the electrons in the Cu 2p orbital undergo spin-orbital and split into Cu 2p 3/2 (930–935 eV) and Cu 2p 1/2 (950–955 eV). The peaks at 940–945 eV are attributed to the satellite peaks of copper [9]. The Cu 2p 3/2 peak can be deconvoluted into two peaks at 933.36 eV and 934.81 eV associated with Cu (I) and Cu (II), respectively. The chemical states of copper on the surface of CuMnAC-1–7 are analyzed based on the binding energy of Cu 2p 3/2 orbital electrons. After the degradation reaction, the Cu2+ content increases from 66.9% to 78.4%, while Cu+ decreases from 33.1% to 21.6%, indicating that copper undergoes an oxidative reaction in the degradation of BPA. The high-resolution XPS spectra of Mn 2p in Fig. 7c display the coexistence of Mn (III) and Mn (IV) on the surface of CuMnAC-1–7, while Mn (II) is present in the post-reaction sample, suggesting that CuMnAC-1–7 acts as an oxidizing agent during the degradation reaction of BPA. The Mn 2p peak can be split into Mn 2p 3/2 (634–646 eV) and Mn 2p 1/2 (650–660 eV), and the satellite peak is located at approximately 647 eV. The Mn 2p 3/2 peak is divided into four peaks at 641.14 eV, 641.76 eV, and 643.0 eV associated with Mn (Ⅱ), Mn (Ⅲ), and Mn (Ⅳ), respectively [66]. The last peak at 644.95 eV does not belong to any valence state of Mn; thus, it should be related to the interaction between Mn and the external environment [6]. Similarly, the binding energies of the electrons in the Mn 2p 3/2 orbital are probed to understand the chemical states of Mn on the surface of CuMnAC-1–7. After the degradation reaction, the Mn3+ content decreases from 45.7% to 34.8% and the Mn4+ content decreases from 37.9% to 35.4%, while 9.4% of Mn2+ appears as the reduction product of Mn. Considering the E0 (Cu2+/Cu+), E0 (Mn3+/Mn2+), E0 (Mn4+/Mn2+), and E0 (Mn4+/Mn3+) are 0.15 V, 1.50 V, 1.29 V, and 0.95 V, respectively. BPA may be oxidized by Mn3+, in which Mn3+ loses electrons and is reduced to Mn2+, whereas Mn4+ with a high redox potential can further react with Cu+ to form Cu2+ and Mn3+ [5]. The rebalance of the Cu-Mn electric pair facilitates the degradation of BPA [45]. The binding energies of O 1 s are at 530.12 eV, 531.46 eV and 532.18 eV, corresponding to the hydroxyl oxygen (OOH), surface-adsorbed oxygen (Oads), and surface lattice oxygen (Olatt), respectively (Fig. 7d). The binding energies and relative contents of O 1 s in the catalyst are compared before and after the degradation reaction. The contents of Oads and Olatt in the fresh CuMnAC-1–7 are 47.9% and 26.9%, respectively. After the reaction, Oads increases to 62.8%, while Olatt decreases to 8.4%. Combined with the relative content of each valence state in Cu and Mn, the reduction of Mn4+ in the lattice results in the conversion of Olatt into Ov, which in turn combined with the Oads on the surface, thus promoting the degradation of BPA [31].

The active species generated by CuMnAC-1–7 in the BPA catalytic degradation system were determined through EPR measurement and free radical trapping experiments. TBA, BQ, TEMP, and AO were used to scavenge·OH [42], O2 ·- [70], 1O2 [32] radicals and oxygen vacancy (Ov) [68]. As shown in Fig. 8a, the degradation rates of BPA were reduced to 98.15%, 36.57%, 32.59%, and 64.93%, respectively, after the addition of TBA, BQ, TEMP, and AO [59]. The degradation of BPA is accelerated by O2 ·-, 1O2, and Ov, while -OH scarcely exerted an inhibitory impact. This indicates that O2 ·-, 1O2, and Ov are generated in the system, consistent with the mechanism of oxidase activity [65]. The experimental results show that BPA oxidation in the CuMnAC-1–7 catalytic system occurs through the free radical pathway.

The involvement of above-mentioned oxidizing species was directly evidenced by conducting EPR measurements using TEMPO and DMPO as spin-trapping reagents. The TEMPO probe is employed to investigate the production of 1O2 with high sensitivity. DMPO effectively captures short-lived free radicals, including Ov and O2 ·-, forming stable intermediates characterized by distinct peaks. As illustrated in Fig. 8b, EPR spectra reveal equivalent signals of O2 ·-, 1O2, and Ov in the electrolytic system. The presence of Ov is consistent with the findings from XPS analysis. These electron-conducted Ov can significantly enhance surface oxygen adsorption and activation, thereby promoting substrate oxidation. In summary, the degradation of BPA by CuMnAC-1–7 involves significant contributions from O2 ·-, 1O2, and Ov in the catalytic reaction. Therefore, it can be hypothesized that Ov facilitate the adsorption of surface oxygen during the reaction, leading to the oxidation of Mn3+ and subsequent production of O2 ·-. Additionally, Ov promotes the conversion of Oads to 1O2 by enhancing electronic conduction between Mn-Cu bimetals [69]. The presence of O2 ·- and 1O2 facilitates BPA oxidation while significantly augmenting the laccase-like activity of the material, thereby promoting its catalytic oxidation.
(1) O2 + e- → O2 ·-
(2) Oads + Ov→ 1O2
(3) O2 ·- + Mn (III)/Cu (Ⅰ) → Mn (Ⅳ)/Cu (II) + O2/Oads
(4) Cu (Ⅰ) + Mn (Ⅳ) → Cu (II) + Mn (III)
(5) O2 ·-/1O2 + BPA → BPAOX
(6) Mn (III) + BPA → BPAOX + Mn (Ⅱ)

The reaction products were recovered by centrifugation and analyzed using LC-MS. The theoretical mass charge ratio of the BPA parent ion is 228.12, while the maximum mass charge ratio of the reaction products is 930.5, indicating that BPA polymerizes during the degradation reaction [20]. Among the reaction products, C15H16O3 with a mass-to-charge ratio of 244.1 is produced when the adjacent hydrogen is substituted with the hydroxyl group (Fig. S4a). C16H16O4 (272.10) is 43.98 (CO2) higher than that of BPA (228.12), corresponding to the BPA product when the phenolic hydroxyl adjacent hydrogen is replaced by carboxyl (Fig. S4b). It indicates the existence of highly oxidized carboxyl groups in the structure. C15H16O3 is probably caused by the reaction between BPA. and molecular water, and C16H16O4 may be caused by the catalysis of CuMnAC-1–7 in the presence of carbonic acid molecules derived from the dissolution of CO2 in water [43,67]. Second, two forms of BPA dimers (C31H30O6 and C40C42O6) are detected in the reaction solution. C31H30O6 with a mass charge ratio of 498.20 is formed by the polymerization of BPA and carboxylated BPA, and C40C42O6 with a mass charge ratio of 618.30 is formed by the polymerization of BPA and hydroxylated BPA (Fig. S4c). In Fig. S4d, C45H46O6 with a mass charge ratio of 680.31 is a trimer of BPA, resulting from the polymerization of one BPA and two hydroxylated BPA molecules. The BPA tetramer with a charge ratio of 906.41 (C60H58O8) consists of one BPA monomer and three hydroxylated BPA molecules (Scheme 1) (Fig. S6e). Based on these results, it can be concluded that the removal of BPA by CuMnAC-1–7 involves laccase-like polymerization [38]. Specifically, the electrons of the BPA benzene ring are stripped by Mn3+ to form phenolic hydroxyl radicals, and the Mn4+ is reduced by Cu+ to from Mn3+ and promote BPA polymerization. The high-charge-density region on the dimer benzene ring may also lose electrons to form free radicals, which are finally polymerized into trimers and tetramers. In contrast to traditional pollutant removal, the mechanism of BPA degradation catalyzed by CuMnAC-1–7 is through oxidative polymerization of aromatic compounds, illuminating the production mechanism of some macromolecular organic matter in nature.

Inspired by the multicopper active sites and electron transfer pathway of the redox of Cu2+/Cu+ of natural laccases, a series of laccase-like nanozymes were synthesized by doping ACs with heterometals. According to the laccase-like activity evaluation, the as-synthesized ACs exhibited greater 2,4-DP oxidation capacity than natural laccases at the same concentration. Moreover, CuMnAC-1–7 shows superior activity and better stability than the other ACs because of the enhanced redox potential related to the electron transportation between Cu2+/Cu+ and Mn4+/Mn3+. Subsequently, CuMnAC-1–7 was used to degrade BPA. Through a series of single-factor experiments, a BPA removal rate of 95% was achieved within 1 h under acidic conditions. The high removal rate and fast reaction time are suitable for practical environmental remediation. Finally, the mechanism of BPA degradation by CuMnAC-1–7 was explored by analyzing the degradation products and free radicals using XPS, LC-MS and EPR. CuMnAC-1–7 separates BPA from water by removing electrons from the benzene ring and catalyzing the polymerization reaction to form polymeric precipitates. This study provides a new strategy for the design and construction of laccase-like nanozymes for EDCs degradation.
